title: Bibi Bhani
hookLine: daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third; tradition says she once held her father's stool steady with her hand

cards: A low wooden stool: short legs, a flat seat, the kind every household had and nobody looked at twice. Tradition says Guru Amar Das sat on one like it each morning while he bathed and prayed. One morning, a leg gave way.
Nobody in the story makes a speech or calls for a carpenter. His daughter is there, and she does the only thing there's time to do.
She slides her hand under the broken corner and holds the seat level, so her father's stillness isn't broken.

teach.h: DAUGHTER, WIFE AND MOTHER OF GURUS.
teach.b: Bibi Bhani's family tree reads like a list of the Gurus. She was the daughter of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru.

She married Bhai Jetha, a young man from Lahore who served in her father's house, and he became Guru Ram Das, the fourth. Their son became Guru Arjan, the fifth. Daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third.
Now the stool. Tradition tells it this way. The leg broke while her father sat in prayer, and Bibi Bhani put her hand beneath the seat and held it.

teach.h: SHE HELD THE STOOL UNTIL IT BLED.
teach.b: She held it so long, the story says, that the wood cut her hand and it bled. She didn't move, and she didn't call out. When Guru Amar Das opened his eyes, he saw the blood on the floor and understood.
Tradition says he was moved, and told her to ask for something. She didn't ask for jewelry, or rest, or praise.

teach.h: SHE ASKED FOR THE GURUSHIP TO STAY.
teach.b: She asked that the Guruship stay in her household. Sikh tradition reads what followed through that moment: from her husband onward, the Gurus came from her family line.

Some tellings say her father warned her the gift would come with suffering, and Sikhs remember that it did. So the story holds two things: devotion that doesn't need an audience, and steadiness as a kind of strength.
Holding something level is quiet work.
But a whole household, and in this story a whole line of Gurus, can rest on a hand that doesn't let go.

how: Sikhs remember Bibi Bhani as the daughter of Guru Amar Das, wife of Guru Ram Das and mother of Guru Arjan, and tell the story of the broken stool as an example of quiet, steady service.

in the story she held it quietly, and her father only saw when he opened his eyes.
when offered a gift, she asked that the Guruship stay in her household
tradition says this was her request.
Guru Ram Das was Bibi Bhani's husband
he was Bhai Jetha, who served in her father's house, before he became the fourth Guru.

games.q: your father is sitting in prayer and the stool under him starts to give way. what do you do?
o: shout so someone brings another stool.
slip your hand under it and hold it level.
gently wake him so he can stand up.
games.why: tradition says Bibi Bhani held it with her hand until it bled, so his prayer wasn't broken.

practice: Rest one hand, palm up, on your knee, as if something small were sitting on it, and feel how much attention it takes to keep a hand still.
Then think of one person carrying something heavy right now, and what you could hold level for them: a ride, a meal, an hour of quiet, an errand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Bibi Bhani. Daughter of Guru Amar Das, wife of Guru Ram Das, mother of Guru Arjan, who, tradition says, held her father's stool steady with her own hand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bibi Bhani; Bibi is a respectful title for a woman.

carryVoice: Your line: she held it steady. Quiet work, with no audience at all. Day eight hundred eight.
